slides.title: Writing Small Numbers in Scientific Notation
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q2 and Q4 are the two halves of today: 10⁻³ is a thousandth, and 0.007 is 7 thousandths, so 0.007 is 7 × 10⁻³. Say that at the reveal. Q1 is yesterday's skill and today's is the mirror image.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
The 3.04 law with base 10: 10⁻ⁿ is 1 over 10ⁿ, and as a decimal it is a 1 in the nth decimal place. 10⁻³ is one thousandth, 0.001, and the 1 is in the thousandths place. Students fill the last two cells. The count to watch: 0.001 has two zeros after the point and the 1 in the THIRD place — the exponent counts places, not zeros.
OFF: 'The exponent tells you which decimal place the 1 is in. Not how many zeros.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Same definition as yesterday; the exponent is negative because the number is less than 1. A red blood cell is 0.000007 m across: the 7 is in the millionths place, so 7 × 10⁻⁶. Then 0.0000672: the first nonzero digit, 6, is in the hundred-thousandths place, so 6.72 × 10⁻⁵ — and it has only four zeros after the point. Reading back: 3.4 × 10⁻⁹ puts the 3 in the billionths place, eight zeros then 34. The rule of thumb: the point moves right n places, the exponent is −n.
OFF: 'Find the first nonzero digit. Its place is the exponent. Everything else is the coefficient.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Same routine as yesterday; the only new thing is that dividing powers of 10 with negative exponents is integer subtraction: 10⁻⁴ ÷ 10⁻⁷ = 10³. Line 1 is the book's collaboration item, and it is sound. Line 2 crosses from a large number to a small one — the state guide's item shape — and the exponent difference 8 − (−4) = 12 does all the work. 'Times smaller' is the same division read the other way: 1.8 × 10⁻⁷ is 4,000 times smaller than 7.2 × 10⁻⁴.
OFF: 'The larger exponent wins. −4 is larger than −7, so 10⁻⁴ is the bigger power.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: A quantity in words, to scientific notation.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The book's oxygen density. Two steps: words to a decimal, decimal to scientific notation. Ask what 'millionths' means as a place before anyone writes.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: 1,332 millionths is 1,332 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.001332. The first nonzero digit, 1, is in the thousandths place: 1.332 × 10⁻³. A board with 1.332 × 10⁻⁶ used the word 'millionths' as the exponent without converting; a board with 1.332 × 10⁻² counted the zeros.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: The book's human hair. 67 hundred-thousandths = 0.00067 = 6.7 × 10⁻⁴. Catches 6.7 × 10⁻⁵ ('hundred-thousandths' used as the exponent) and 6.7 × 10⁻³ (zeros counted).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The book's collaboration item. Ask which number is larger before anyone divides — the exponents decide, and −4 beats −7.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: 7.2 ÷ 1.8 = 4 and 10⁻⁴ ÷ 10⁻⁷ = 10³ (−4 minus −7 is 3). So 4,000 times. A board with 4 stopped at the coefficients; a board with 4 × 10⁻³ subtracted the exponents the wrong way (−7 − (−4)); a board with 40 wrote 10 for 10³. Confirm: 0.00072 ÷ 0.00000018 = 4,000.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: The book's practice item. 5.2 ÷ 2.6 = 2 and 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁸ = 10⁵: 200,000. A board with 2 × 10⁻⁵ subtracted the wrong way.

slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written. The state guide's task for this benchmark. Full credit: the thicker line, the factor 3, and a value strictly between 0.02 and 0.06 written in either form. A student who answers '3 times thinner' for the first line has the comparison right and the direction reversed — mark it right only if the sentence says which line is which. A student who gives 4 × 10⁻¹ has the coefficient right and the power wrong (that is 0.4 in, thicker than both).
